comments.author: @caiofernandes3727
comments.text:
I believe the main difference was that slavery in the United States was largely confined to the South, whereas Brazil was essentially one vast coffee or sugarcane plantation across almost its entire territory, for a much longer period and on a much larger scale. Brazil did have colonization based on small landholdings in the southern part of the country, where settlers could acquire land at little or no cost, but this was not enough to lay the foundations for an industrial middle class in the 19th century.
Furthermore, the lack of coal, which was the driving force behind the First Industrial Revolution, the geographical challenges described in the video, and the lack of access to two oceans also had a significant impact. There is one more factor that I consider less important, but which is related to cultural aspects: although I am a practicing Catholic Brazilian, I believe that the Protestant work ethic played an important role in the early stages of capitalism. Today, however, I consider this factor largely irrelevant.

comments.author: @atlas567
comments.text: Geography can be an obstacle, but not a major one—at least not in Brazil. Portugal did a great deal in Brazil—more, in fact, than England did for the United States. Brazil already possessed hospital networks known as *Santa Casa de Misericórdia*, as well as shipyards for vessel construction—including the very caravels and galleons Portugal used for conquests and warfare. There were also banks to provide financing and loans. During the reign of Dom Pedro II—after Brazil had gained its independence—universities and even medical schools were established. Furthermore, Brazil was the second-largest destination for Europeans during the great wave of European immigration between 1870 and 1930, trailing only the United States; it was also the primary destination for Japanese immigrants. Aside from the Japanese, Brazil did not permit immigration from Asia or Africa; it was only after the Second World War that the country began to accept Jews, Christian Arabs, Chinese, Koreans, and other Asians and Africans. These immigrants settled almost exclusively in the South and Southeast regions of Brazil, where the climate is quite similar to that of the American South and parts of the U.S. Midwest—a fact that makes the contrast between these regions and the rest of the country clearly visible. However, the factor that most hindered Brazil’s progress was socialism. The *coup d’état* that overthrew the monarchy and established the republic also introduced a form of socialism—known at the time as "positivism"—which persisted until the end of the military regime in 1985. Socialism returned in 1994 under Fernando Henrique Cardoso, and today, under Lula, it borders on communism. This is Brazil’s greatest bottleneck.
